text: Subscribe to skip adsAdvertisementHistoryIs This the First Corporate Psychopath?A historical study makes a compelling caseJCBy Jake Currie4:00 PM CDT on October 22, 2026Add Nautilus to GoogleIn 1629, the Dutch East India Company ship Batavia set sail for Java in the East Indies, but never made it to its final destination. Instead, it ran aground on the Abrolhos Islands, a chain of small islands off the west coast of Australia. Some 200 souls survived, but soon discovered both food and fresh water were lacking. To compound problems, the ship’s officers absconded in a sail boat pointed toward Java to get help, leaving a power vacuum. That vacuum was filled by Jeronimus Cornelisz, a junior merchant on his first voyage who had abandoned his wife and child, and his reign was barbarous. According to a new historical case study published in the Asian Journal of Business Ethics, it also bore all the hallmarks of corporate psychopathy—perhaps the first such instance.  Read more: “Are You Smart Enough to Avoid Falling for “Corporate Bullsh*t”?”Subscribe to skip adsAdvertisement
